questions.problem: A linear system of ODEs has the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}=[1,\,-1]^{T}.$ Two linearly independent eigenvectors of the system's matrix are ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ After shifting using $u=x-{x}^{∗},$ the system becomes ${u}^{′}=Au.$ Which of the following is **guaranteed** to be an eigenvector of the matrix $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
After shifting a linear system, the eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenvectors remain unchanged.

Thus, the matrix $A$ in the shifted system has the same eigenvectors as the system's matrix in the original coordinates. These eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ or any nonzero vectors that are parallel to them.

Among the given options, the only vector that is nonzero and is guaranteed to be parallel to either ${v}_{1}$ or ${v}_{2}$ is the vector $-{v}_{2}.$

questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)-4x(t)+y(t)+4 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+2y(t)-6\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of ODEs above. An equilibrium point of the system is $[2,\,0]^{T}.$ Which of the following is the system obtained by shifting this equilibrium to the origin?
questions.worked_solution:
To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,x=u+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

In coordinate form, this can be written as follows:

$$
x(t)=u(t)+2,\,y(t)=v(t),\,{x}^{′}(t)={u}^{′}(t),\,{v}^{′}(t)={y}^{′}(t)
$$

Let's now substitute these into the given system.

- Substituting into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{2}(t)-4x(t)+y(t)+4 \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =(u(t)+2)^{2}-4(u(t)+2)+v(t)+4 \\  & ={u}^{2}(t)+4u(t)+4-4u(t)-8+v(t)+4 \\  & ={u}^{2}(t)+v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =3x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+2y(t)-6 \\ {v}^{′}(t) & =3(u(t)+2)-{v}^{2}(t)+2v(t)-6 \\  & =3u(t)+6-{v}^{2}(t)+2v(t)-6 \\  & =3u(t)+2v(t)-{v}^{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)={u}^{2}(t)+v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=3u(t)+2v(t)-{v}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+5x(t)+2y(t)+6 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+4y(t)+6\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of ODEs above. An equilibrium point of the system is $[-2,\,0]^{T}.$ Which of the following is the system obtained by shifting this equilibrium to the origin?
questions.worked_solution:
To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,x=u+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

In coordinate form, this can be written as follows:

$$
x(t)=u(t)-2,\,y(t)=v(t),\,{x}^{′}(t)={u}^{′}(t),\,{v}^{′}(t)={y}^{′}(t).
$$

Let's now substitute these into the given system.

- Substituting into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{2}(t)+5x(t)+2y(t)+6 \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =(u(t)-2)^{2}+5(u(t)-2)+2v(t)+6 \\  & =({u}^{2}(t)-4u(t)+4)+5u(t)-10+2v(t)+6 \\  & ={u}^{2}(t)+u(t)+2v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =3x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+4y(t)+6 \\ {v}^{′}(t) & =3(u(t)-2)-{v}^{2}(t)+4v(t)+6 \\  & =3u(t)-6-{v}^{2}(t)+4v(t)+6 \\  & =3u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)+4v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)={u}^{2}(t)+u(t)+2v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=3u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)+4v(t)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A system of ODEs has an unstable saddle point at ${x}^{∗}.$ The system is then shifted using $u=x-{x}^{∗}.$ Which of the following best describes the point $(0,0)$ for the shifted system?
questions.worked_solution:
Shifting does not alter the local behavior near an equilibrium. So, the equilibrium retains its original classification (saddle, node, spiral, center, etc.).

Recall that the shift moves the equilibrium to the origin.

Thus, the equilibrium at $(0,0)$ in the shifted system has the same classification as ${x}^{∗}$ in the original system.

Therefore, the correct answer is "An unstable saddle point".
